lead: Layering splits a network job into levels, so a change at one level leaves the others alone. Each level talks to its peer at the far end and hands data down through a clear interface. Optics is the bottom level and carries bits for every layer above. Asynchronous Transfer Mode (ATM) is a fixed-cell layer-2 design that once promised voice, video and data on one optical pipe. Only a few syllabi teach this topic. The chapter maps layers, data units and ATM, and shows why IP won.
prereq: You need: circuit and packet transmission modes (Optical network concepts) and the SONET/SDH frame (SONET/SDH).

blocks.text: The Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) model has seven layers. Each layer adds its own header (and sometimes a trailer) to what it receives from above and passes the result, its protocol data unit (PDU), down.

items: Application: user services such as web and e-mail.
Presentation: data format, compression and encryption.
Session: starting and ending a dialogue.
Transport: end-to-end delivery, ordering and flow control.
Network: addressing and routing across many links, as IP does.
Data link: frames on one link, with error checks.
Physical: bits on the medium: wavelength, connector, power and line code.

blocks.text: The PDU is a bit at the physical layer, a frame at the data link layer, a packet at the network layer, a segment at the transport layer for TCP (a datagram for UDP) and a message at the application layer. The TCP/IP model folds session and presentation into the application and has four layers: application, transport, internet and link. Optics works at the physical layer: a photodiode does not read an IP address.

IP can ride on SONET/SDH, on Ethernet, or straight on WDM lightpaths (WDM networks). Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) puts a short fixed label in front of each packet, so routers switch on the label rather than the full IP header; generalized MPLS (GMPLS) extends the label idea to time slots, wavelengths and fibers.

sections.h3: ATM cells, layers and service classes

blocks.text: ATM sends everything in cells of 53 bytes: a 5-byte header and a 48-byte payload. At the user-network interface the header holds a 4-bit generic flow control field, an 8-bit virtual path identifier (VPI), a 16-bit virtual channel identifier (VCI), a 3-bit payload type, a 1-bit cell loss priority and an 8-bit header error control byte; inside the network the flow control bits join the VPI, giving 12 bits. Short fixed cells keep voice delay small, because a voice sample never waits behind a long packet, and they let hardware switch with one table lookup per cell.

ATM has three layers. The physical layer moves cells over SONET/SDH or fiber. The ATM layer adds and removes the header and switches cells by VPI/VCI. The ATM adaptation layer (AAL) cuts user data into 48-byte pieces and rebuilds it at the far end. AAL1 carries constant-bit-rate voice and circuit emulation, AAL2 carries compressed voice, and AAL5 carries data: it adds padding and then an 8-byte trailer (with the length and a CRC-32), so that data + pad + trailer fill a whole number of 48-byte payloads and the trailer sits in the last 8 bytes of the last cell.

Service classes give quality of service (QoS). Constant bit rate (CBR) is a fixed rate with tight delay, like a call. Real-time variable bit rate (VBR-rt) varies in rate but keeps delay tight, like compressed video. Non-real-time VBR (VBR-nrt) varies with looser delay. Available bit rate (ABR) shares spare capacity using feedback. Unspecified bit rate (UBR) gives no guarantee, like a file download.

ATM lost to IP and Ethernet. IP was already on every computer, Ethernet was cheap and kept getting faster, and ATM paid a cell tax of 5 header bytes on every 48 payload bytes plus AAL padding. IP over WDM, often with MPLS, now carries most backbone traffic; ATM survives mainly in older access and telephone networks, and its virtual-circuit labels and QoS classes live on in MPLS.

examples.question: An IP packet of 1500 bytes is sent over AAL5, which adds an 8-byte trailer and pads the result to whole 48-byte cell payloads. (a) How many cells are needed? (b) How many pad bytes are added? (c) How many bytes go on the link? (d) What is the efficiency? (e) How long does this take on an STM-1 carrying 149.76 Mb/s of cells?
steps: (a) Data plus trailer = 1500 + 8 = 1508 bytes. Cells = ⌈1508/48⌉ = ⌈31.42⌉ = 32 cells.
(b) 32 payloads hold 32 × 48 = 1536 bytes, so the pad is 1536 − 1508 = 28 bytes, placed before the trailer.
(d) Efficiency = 1500/1696 = 0.8844, or 88.4 percent. The headers cost 32 × 5 = 160 bytes and pad plus trailer 36 bytes.
examples.answer: 32 cells with 28 pad bytes, 1696 bytes on the link, 88.4 percent efficiency, 90.6 µs on the STM-1 payload.

traps: Count the 5-byte header: a 48-byte payload costs 53 bytes on the link, not 48.
Add the 8-byte AAL5 trailer before dividing by 48: a 90-byte packet seems to need ⌈90/48⌉ = 2 cells, but 90 + 8 = 98 bytes need 3.
AAL5 pads first and puts the trailer last, in the final 8 bytes of the last cell; the trailer is not between data and pad.
VPI names the path and VCI the channel inside it; do not swap them. AAL1 carries constant-bit-rate voice and AAL5 carries data.
The transport PDU is a segment for TCP but a datagram for UDP; a frame belongs to the data link layer.

quiz.q: Name the seven OSI layers from top to bottom.
quiz.a: Application, presentation, session, transport, network, data link, physical.

quiz.q: List the five ATM service classes.
quiz.a: CBR, VBR-rt, VBR-nrt, ABR and UBR.

quiz.q: Why are ATM cells short and fixed in size?
quiz.a: Short cells keep the packetization and queueing delay of voice small; a fixed size lets hardware switch every cell with one simple lookup.

quiz.q: Which layer does optics work at, and what is its data unit?
quiz.a: The physical layer; its data unit is the bit.

quiz.q: A 600-byte IP packet uses AAL5 with an 8-byte trailer and 48-byte payloads. Find the cells, the pad and the link bytes.
quiz.a: 608/48 = 12.67, so 13 cells. Pad = 13 × 48 − 608 = 16 bytes. Link bytes = 13 × 53 = 689. Efficiency = 600/689 = 87.1 percent.

quiz.q: Why did ATM lose to IP and Ethernet?
quiz.a: IP was already on every computer, Ethernet was cheap and kept getting faster, and ATM added cell overhead (5 of every 53 bytes plus padding) and connection set-up complexity. MPLS later gave IP networks ATM’s label switching and traffic control.

quiz.q: A voice call needs tight delay but a file transfer can wait. Which ATM classes fit each, and why?
quiz.a: Voice: CBR, or VBR-rt for compressed voice, because they bound delay and delay variation. File transfer: ABR or UBR (VBR-nrt for bursty data with a contract), because they accept variable delay and use spare capacity.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, IP and MPLS over DWDM form the core of metro and backbone networks, with OTN switching underneath. Researchers place the control plane in software-defined networking controllers. Search for GMPLS, MPLS-TP, segment routing and OTN switching.
